newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia election flawed but overall fair - OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Croatia election flawed but overall fair - OSCE.

text.p: Croatia's elections were free and fair overall but voting in a Serb enclave was riddled with irregularities and opposition parties lacked proper access to the main state-run media, the OSCE said on Wednesday.

In the April 13-14 regional elections, President Franjo Tudjman's nationalist HDZ party regained majorities in almost all 21 county assemblies and most town councils but lost to or deadlocked with opposition coalitions in the biggest cities.
Almost 200 observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe scrutinised the vote which included the former rebel region of Eastern Slavonia for the first time.

Eastern Slavonia, one of the areas where local Serbs seized power in a 1991 revolt against Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia, will come back under state rule this summer after a transitional period as a U..N. protectorate.

The OSCE report, obtained by Reuters in Zagreb, zeroed in on technical problems that delayed the opening of polling stations in Eastern Slavonia for hours on Sunday, forcing U.N. officials to give the Serbs an extra day to vote.

"Problems included last minute changes of election regulations and late notification of the changed regulations to polling commissions and voters; inaccuracies in voter lists; late delivery and absence of materials including ballots and ballot boxes; and late opening of polling stations," it said.

The U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) said the second day of balloting went smoothly and some Western observers including U.S. Ambassador Peter Galbraith agreed, saying most Serbs who had wanted to vote did so.
"But according to (our) observers, significant problems persisted into the second day of voting," the OSCE report said.

"(These) included late opening of significant numbers of polling stations, widespread reports of lack of ballot papers or delivery of the wrong ballot papers in many polling stations, and in some cases the distribution and use of misprinted ballot papers.
"Of 90 observer reports so far, one third of them reflect serious problems," the report said.
It added: "The ... problems seemed to be the result of an unrealistic time schedule imposed by political considerations at the expense of efficient election management."

UNTAES mission chief Jacques Klein approved Croatia's request to have the enclave vote on the same day as the elections elsewhere in Croatia to underscore its pending reversion to central state control.

UNTAES also came under fire from Croatian refugee voters who bemoaned its decision to speed up voting by allowing Serbs to cast ballots without being registered, as long as they produced some form of identification.
Croatian refugees contend that UNTAES' relaxation of voting rules might have produced fraudulent Serb party majorities in towns where Croats once lived and now hope to resettle.
UNTAES hoped to have voting results by Friday. "It will be up to UNTAES to decide on certification of the election in the region," the OSCE noted, without making any recommendation.

In the rest of Croatia, the election was "generally efficient" -- freer and fairer than voting for the national parliament in 1995 but "some significant issues of concern" remained, the OSCE report said.
Observers found balloting secrecy insufficient in some 20 percent of polling stations, especially in rural locales, and there were some instances of illegal proxy voting.

Non-partisan civic observers were still prevented from monitoring voting and the state-run major media, especially television, gave short shrift to opposition parties while boosting the HDZ with exhaustive and fawning coverage.
